Ancient History.Prehistoric India:
INTRODUCTION
Prehistory refers to the long phase of human existence before the invention of writing. Since literary records are absent, knowledge of this period is reconstructed from archaeological evidence such as stone tools, habitation sites, bones, plant remains and rock paintings. It is the earliest stage of human cultural evolution and shows the gradual transition from food gathering to food production.

PALEOLITHIC AGE
The Paleolithic Age or Old Stone Age is the earliest phase of prehistory. It broadly extended from about 2.5 million years ago to around 10000 BCE. Human life in this phase was marked by complete dependence on nature, hunting, scavenging and food gathering.

FEATURES
• Stone tools were the main cultural remains and were made mostly of quartzite and other hard stones
• Human beings lived as nomads and moved in search of food and water
• There was no agriculture, pottery or permanent settlement
• Caves and rock shelters were used at some places for habitation
• Fire was known in the later stages and helped in cooking, warmth and protection

The Paleolithic Age is generally divided into Lower, Middle and Upper Paleolithic on the basis of tool typology.

In the Lower Paleolithic phase, large tools such as hand axes, cleavers and choppers were common. In the Middle Paleolithic phase, flake tools became more frequent and tool making became more refined. In the Upper Paleolithic phase, blade tools, bone tools and artistic expressions became more visible, indicating a higher degree of cultural development.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is famous for rock shelters and rock paintings and provides evidence of long human occupation
• Hunsgi in Karnataka shows settlement near water sources and availability of raw material for tools
• Kurnool caves in Andhra Pradesh are important for cave habitation evidence
• Belan Valley in Uttar Pradesh shows a long cultural sequence from the Stone Age onward
• Didwana in Rajasthan and Soan Valley in the north west are also significant Paleolithic regions

MESOLITHIC AGE
The Mesolithic Age or Middle Stone Age represents a transitional phase between Paleolithic and Neolithic. It broadly dates from about 10000 BCE to 6000 BCE, though regional variations existed. This phase developed in the context of climatic improvement after the end of the Ice Age.

FEATURES
• Microliths or very small stone tools are the most distinctive feature of this phase
• These small tools were often fitted into wooden or bone handles to make composite implements
• Human groups continued hunting and gathering, but fishing and collection of a wider range of food resources became important
• Semi sedentary settlements began to appear in some areas
• Animal domestication began in an early form, especially dog
• Human burials with grave goods indicate the development of social customs and belief systems

The Mesolithic phase did not represent a complete break from the Paleolithic past. Rather, it was a phase of adaptation and experimentation that prepared the ground for food production.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bagor in Rajasthan is one of the most important Mesolithic sites and gives evidence of animal domestication
• Langhnaj in Gujarat shows hunting, food gathering and human skeletal remains
• Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha in Uttar Pradesh are important for burial evidence
• Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh reflects continuity of microlithic culture

NEOLITHIC AGE
The Neolithic Age or New Stone Age marks a decisive turning point in human history because it introduced food production. In the Indian subcontinent, Neolithic cultures appeared in different regions at different times from about 7000 BCE onward in some areas.

FEATURES
• Agriculture and animal domestication became the basis of life
• Polished stone tools replaced the earlier rough stone tools in many areas
• Permanent settlements and village communities developed
• Pottery, weaving and storage of grain became common
• Social organisation became more stable because people began to live in settled communities
• Grinding stones, pestles and sickles indicate food processing and cultivation

The Neolithic phase marks the shift from a food gathering economy to a food producing economy. This transformation is often described as the Neolithic Revolution because it fundamentally changed human life.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Mehrgarh in the north west is one of the earliest farming settlements of the subcontinent and shows wheat and barley cultivation, domesticated animals and early craft activity
• Burzahom in Kashmir is famous for pit dwellings and distinctive burial practices
• Gufkral in Kashmir is another important Neolithic site
• Chirand in Bihar gives evidence of settled life, agriculture and animal husbandry
• Hallur, Maski and related sites indicate the spread of Neolithic culture in South India

REGIONAL PATTERN
Neolithic culture did not emerge uniformly across India. In the north west, early farming is seen at Mehrgarh. In Kashmir, pit dwellings are a striking feature. In eastern India, sites such as Chirand reflect farming and village life. In South India, ash mounds, cattle keeping and polished stone axes are important clues to Neolithic development.

SIGNIFICANCE
Prehistoric India shows the long process through which human beings moved from mere survival to organised community life. The shift from hunting and gathering to agriculture led to food surplus, population growth and stable settlements. This in turn created the basis for craft production, social differentiation and eventually the rise of more complex cultures and civilizations. Thus, prehistoric developments laid the broad foundation for later urban civilization in the Indian subcontinent.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Paleolithic culture is identified mainly through large stone tools and hunting gathering economy
• Mesolithic culture is identified through microliths and transitional subsistence pattern
• Neolithic culture is identified through agriculture, animal domestication, polished tools and settled life
• Bhimbetka is important for rock art and long continuity of occupation
• Mehrgarh is crucial for earliest farming evidence in the subcontinent
• Burzahom is known for pit dwellings, a favourite factual area in competitive exams

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often mixes up microliths, polished tools and agriculture. Microliths are mainly Mesolithic, while polished stone tools and settled agriculture belong to the Neolithic phase.
